summary: Irvine is one of the largest master-planned cities ever built in the United States — nearly the entire 65.9-square-mile footprint was designed from scratch on the old Irvine Ranch, which means the street grid, open-space network, and commercial nodes didn't evolve organically but were laid out with almost eerie intentionality. That planning shows: over 16,000 acres of parks and preserved open space thread through the city, and a network of off-street bike and pedestrian trails connects neighborhoods to shopping centers, schools, and employment clusters without forcing you onto arterial roads. And Irvine is genuinely a job center, not a bedroom community — Broadcom, Edwards Lifesciences, Blizzard Entertainment, and the University of California, Irvine anchor a deep bench of tech, biomedical, gaming, and higher-education employers, so switching jobs without switching commutes is plausible. Still, buying is a stretch: a median home at $1,115,400 sits at roughly 8.6 times the $129,647 median household income, pushing ownership well past conventional lending thresholds even for high earners. The climate is relentlessly mild — 74°F average highs and over nine hours of daily sunshine year-round, with the Santa Ana Mountains framing eastern views and the coast about a fifteen-minute drive west. The tradeoff is that all that planning delivers convenience and green space but relatively little grit or surprise — Irvine functions like a beautifully optimized machine whose precision is either its greatest asset or its most defining limitation, depending on what you need a city to be.
